items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Friday, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin holding unprecedented trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announcing that Türkiye's homegrown Kizilelma unmanned fighter jet has entered the Turkish Armed Forces' inventory after years of development, the UN's top court ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims in 2017, marking the first time it has held a state responsible for genocide, and reports that Grand Theft Auto VI has received widespread acclaim following its global release. Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for unprecedented trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China. The three leaders delivered remarks during a media session lasting approximately 15 minutes before proceeding to closed-door discussions. Their public remarks addressed nuclear disarmament, global security and the Russia-Ukraine war, among other issues. Trump said the US, Russia and China are "uniquely positioned" to discuss reducing nuclear weapons and lowering the risk of their use during trilateral talks with the Chinese and Russian presidents. Xi said that "positive interactions" among China, the US and Russia were not an "option but a must" as he met with his US and Russian counterparts. In the meeting, Putin said the three powers could contribute to strengthening global stability if they cooperate constructively. In a joint statement titled "Declaration toward Peace" following the talks, the Chinese, Russian and US presidents agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. ... - UN court rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya in 1st such ruling against a state The UN's top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims in 2017, marking the first time it has held a state responsible for genocide. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar responsible for genocide during military operations in northern Rakhine State by a vote of 9-6. Reading the judgment, International Court of Justice President Judge Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide." UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed the landmark ruling.

items.title: Fed's Paulson signals more rate hikes, says inflation remains too high - The Economic Times
items.excerpt: , ETMarkets.com Last Updated: Nov 20, 2026, 09:58:00 AM IST Synopsis Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson called for further US interest rate hikes to bring inflation under control, citing strong economic growth and a resilient labour market. Her hawkish remarks come ahead of the Fed's December policy meeting. Agencies Philadelphia Fed's Anna Paulson backs further rate hikes as inflation remains stubborn. Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said the US central bank needs to raise interest rates further to bring inflation under control, arguing that price pressures remain too high despite an otherwise robust economy. Speaking after a speech at an event organised by the Money Marketeers of New York University on Thursday, Paulson said stronger economic growth and a labour market at full employment meant inflation should remain the priority for monetary policymakers.

items.title: AI is fueling "disturbingly high" inflation, Chicago Fed president says - CBS News
items.excerpt: Updated on: November 19, 2026 / 6:40 PM EST / CBS News The boom in AI data center construction is adding to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation, with the sector's massive business investment indirectly contributing to rising service prices, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday. "The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy," Goolsbee said. "I find it hard to look at it any other way when you are getting major business investment, almost an unprecedented level of business investment." Goolsbee, who will become a voting member of the interest rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in January, declined to forecast the central bank's next moves on interest rates. But he said the Fed's decisions will be determined by whether U.S. inflation is on track to return to the central bank's annual 2% target. "The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%," Goolsbee added.

items.title: Higher fuel prices seep into core inflation - Dallasfed.org
items.excerpt: Alexander Chudik, Lutz Kilian and Xiaoqing Zhou November 19, 2026 Fuel prices have been on a wild ride since late February 2026, when military strikes on Iran set off sharp moves in oil and fuel markets. Retail gasoline prices aside, the U.S. retail diesel price reached an all-time high, the jet fuel price is near its previous peak, and the heating oil price has set a new record. The U.S. price of natural gas, meanwhile, has barely budged. The fuel price surge has been very uneven. Diesel prices in particular moved sharply higher. Diesel is the fuel of the freight economy. Trucks, trains, ships and farm equipment run on it, which means its price may potentially touch the cost of moving nearly everything consumers buy. The price gap between diesel and gasoline has widened significantly in recent months. On Sept. 22, 2026, the national average retail price of diesel reached $6.53 per gallon, about 70 percent above its level at the end of February (compared with a 50 percent rise for retail gasoline). The diesel rise surpassed the fuel’s previous record set in 2022 (Chart 1). Prices have eased only modestly, to about $6.31 as of the end of October. Consumers experience these prices directly at the pump and indirectly on their utility bills. But fuel prices may also work their way into the prices of other goods and services, from airline tickets to paper towels. Economists call these "second-round effects," and they matter for the Federal Reserve because they show up in core inflation, an inflation measure that excludes food and energy. Policymakers watch core inflation closely to gauge underlying price pressures. Our estimates suggest that higher fuel prices added between 20 and 60 basis points to 12-month core inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, as of September 2026. If fuel prices simply held at their current levels, that contribution would gradually decline by about 30 basis points by the end of 2027.

items.title: Fed’s Jefferson says AI boosting inflation, productivity impact possible ’in the future’ By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The rapid artificial intelligence buildout is putting upward pressure on US inflation through its impact on demand, Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Thursday, with possible productivity gains that could help ease price pressures only coming "in the future." In prepared remarks to a Brazilian central bank conference, Jefferson said the AI boom is the sort of shock that could influence both demand and supply, but at different points in time. "On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products," Jefferson said. "Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation." Productivity improvements from the new technology could put downward pressure on prices, but only "in the future," Jefferson said, without estimating a timeline. Jefferson’s prepared remarks did not mention his current interest-rate outlook.

items.title: The 120th Congress Shapes Up - RealClearPolitics
items.excerpt: Published Nov. 20, 2026 • Read time: 6m ... In the final weeks before the holidays, members of Congress are packing up their offices and delivering their final floor speeches. Democrats are war-gaming the next two years amid caution not to rest on their laurels; Republican frustrations are bubbling into shouting matches on the Senate floor. And both parties are already grappling with how to handle the power swap coming in January. Incumbent Democrats appear to be already preparing for executive branch investigations. House Oversight Committee ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia of California is expected to lead the powerful committee starting in January. This week, he sent letters to a baker’s dozen of Trump allies and family members warning them to preserve documents. In a press release, he described his actions as “just the beginning.” But the White House is already pushing back. White House Counsel Will Scharf wrote a letter, first obtained by Politico, back to Garcia reminding him that minority members cannot enforce document requests. He also didn’t appreciate the tone. He cited one letter from Rep. Richard Blumenthal that he said accused Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin of “unprecedented violence.” Another from Rep. Robert Scott to Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling suggested that employees are burning documents before Democrats take control. “All drip with an animus or pettiness revealing that the purpose of those letters is not legitimate oversight but to harass and aggrandize,” Scharf wrote. But the tables will turn in January. Scharf said the White House would comply with the law about responding to committee chairs, but he left open a potential loophole. He said the White House would work requests “in furtherance of a legitimate legislative purpose.” “Our commitment in this respect, though, is of course colored and qualified by the ‘pettiness’ promised by one potential incoming Chair and numerous other similar statements, which we believe indicate that you and your colleagues may inappropriately seek to use oversight investigations to harass individuals with meritless claims,” he concluded. Scharf also sent a memo to the entire administration ordering federal workers to first receive permission from the Office of White House Counsel or the Office of Legislative Affairs before appearing before any congressional committee. But incoming Democrats say they’ll be less focused on investigations and toeing the party line, whatever it turns out to be. ... Senate Democrats are already wading through the first wave of party infighting in their leadership elections. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer to be the Senate majority leader. If he wins, it could be a referendum on the establishment within the party. But either leader will inherit a sizeable majority and even broader ideological differences, all the way from moderate Democrats in red states to Democrat Socialists. On the other side of the aisle, Republicans are equally divided on how they will handle their minority. Reporters could hear outgoing Sen. John Cornyn yelling at fellow Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, apparently over Cornyn’s opposition to a federal judge nominee. But the ire spilled into someone “for ending my career!” Cornyn shouted, according to The Washington Sun. Cornyn will leave the halls next month, but Cruz will remain. And he’s gearing up for battle. “You know, it’s amazing on the campaign trail the Democrats talked about affordability all day long, and the day after the election, they immediately turned to nonstop political warfare,” Cruz told reporters on Wednesday. “I think the people of Texas and the people of this country are in two very difficult years because of the radicals.” Sen. Ron Johnson told reporters he was aggravated at Democrats being “obnoxiously obstructionist” this week. Next year, the GOP will be the professional thorn in the majority’s side. Sen. Katie Britt of Alabama urged a different approach. She told RealClearPolitics her main tactic will be to look for compromises and restore some measure of good faith between the parties. Her negotiations during the government shutdown last year might work in her favor.

items.excerpt: ## 1. JAZZWRLD and GL CEEJAY celebrate Grammy recognition with Davido South African producer JAZZWRLD and musician GL CEEJAY have found themselves part of a Grammy conversation that extends well beyond local music, with their contributions to Davido’s album ORIADÉ earning recognition on the international stage. The 13-track album, released on July 31, 2026, has been nominated for Best Global Music Album at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards. Its mix of international collaborators reflects Afrobeats’ continued reach across borders, with the two South Africans among those credited on the project. ... ## 9. Beyoncé reaches 100 Grammy nominations Beyoncé has added another historic milestone to an already record-breaking Grammy career, becoming the first artist to reach 100 nominations. Her latest recognition comes for Morning Dew (Donk), which has been nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 2027 Grammy Awards. The song was released in July ahead of the 20th anniversary of her album “B’Day”. The milestone adds to a career that began collecting Grammy recognition with Destiny’s Child in 2000, when the group earned nominations for “Bills, Bills, Bills”. Beyoncé remains the most-awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins. She will compete in the R&B Solo Performance category against Kehlani for “Out the Window”, Victoria Monét for “Let Me”, Jill Scott for “Pressha” and Tems for “What You Need”. The 2027 ceremony is scheduled for February 7 in Los Angeles.

items.excerpt: Friday, November 20 is the most crowded release day of the month — five notable films in cinemas and at least seven new titles on streaming, all landing while Ramayana plays its third weekend and the 57th IFFI opens in Goa. ... In cinemas today The headline Indian release is O.M: Operation Mole, Rajkumar Periasamy’s Tamil action thriller with Dhanush as an undercover officer, Mammootty as a smuggling kingpin, Sai Pallavi as an IPS officer and Sreeleela — releasing in Tamil, Telugu and Hindi. Its advance booking closed at a reported Rs 16.56 crore, the strongest pre-sales of any new release this week; our full advance-booking report is here: https://filmverse.in/om-operation-mole-advance-booking-16-56-crore-dhanush-mammootty-november-20/ Sharing the day is Dulquer Salmaan’s Telugu drama Aakasamlo Oka Tara, in which Satvika Veeravalli plays Kalpana, a district topper whose astronaut dream survives an early marriage. In Tamil, Keerthy Suresh’s courtroom drama Sathyavan Savithiri arrives with a U/A certificate — our release-eve report is here: https://filmverse.in/sathyavan-savithiri-release-november-20-keerthy-suresh-mysskin-ua-certificate/ The Hindi belt gets Amit Sadh’s crime drama Pratap and the comedy Party Animals, while horror fans have Jackie Shroff and Sharad Kelkar in Kaali Kheti. Hollywood brings two event films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and Japan’s Godzilla Minus Zero, delayed from November 6 — though premium-format shows for both are limited because Ramayana still holds most IMAX screens in India.
